bradley.label: Bradley Berkman
bradley.summary: I make complexity legible enough to act on.

paragraphs.p1: Hey, I'm Bradley. I run Brain in a Vat Group, which includes a [music promotions](record:music-practice) agency, a [systems and AI](record:systems-consulting) consulting practice, and a product studio focused on [software](record:product-studio).
paragraphs.p2: Before founding BiV, I launched and led the music-promotions division at INFAMOUS PR. Prior to that, I studied Philosophy, Politics, and Law, with a Music Industry minor, at the University of Southern California.
paragraphs.p3: Beyond my work, I enjoy: raving, arguing about the philosophy of consciousness, trading sheep for brick over a Catan board, and the ongoing search for New York City's finest hamburger.
paragraphs.p4: Thanks for checking out my portfolio!

infamous.label: INFAMOUS PR
infamous.summary: Launching an experimental suite of new-media services that grew into a department I ran within electronic music's premiere PR agency.

paragraphs.p1: By 2021, INFAMOUS PR had spent fifteen years at the top of electronic music PR, with a roster including Live Nation, TheDoLab, Teksupport, Pabst Blue Ribbon, Red Bull, Rockstar Games, RÜFÜS DU SOL, Carl Craig, Pete Tong, CircoLoco Records, Desert Hearts, and Dirtybird.
paragraphs.p2: The agency specialized in long, narrative driven campaigns, which often narrowed campaigns to albums, tours, and larger activations, while the incentives of streaming economy were shifting dance music's release cycle towards ephemeral, less narrative oriented singles and EPs. There was lots of inbound business from the agency's clients wanting to market these releases, but INFAMOUS was turning the campaigns away — without a strong narrative and a multi-month retainer, these sorts of campaigns can be difficult to land traditional media placements. I was hired to solve this problem.
paragraphs.p3: The services were shaped by client feedback, evolving each campaign — DSP playlist promotion first, then additional services including radio plugging, DJ promotion, YouTube distribution, and social media post seeding and influencer campaigns.
paragraphs.p4: It is also where I first learned the lesson that has continued to appear throughout my career: the shape and feel of the work is itself something I can improve.

infamous-service-evolution.purpose: Show how the fourth department and its service offering developed release by release.

music-practice.label: Brain in a Vat Music Promotions Agency
music-practice.summary: Brain in a Vat Music Promotions is the boutique digital marketing agency behind some of today's most influential dance music releases.

paragraphs.p1:
I offer artists and record labels a suite of services that include:
- Playlist promotion
- Radio plugging
- Social media seeding and influencer campaigns
- Press campaigns
paragraphs.p2: Regardless of the services, each campaign is the same core process.
paragraphs.p3: Before taking on a campaign, listen to the music to map it sonically, understand the context surrounding the music, like the current state of affairs for the artist, record label, and relevant genres. Then, I need to talk to my client to understand their goals for the release. They're trying to influence the outcome of their upcoming release, and this can mean many things for many different artists and record labels. BiV takes a unique stance against the industry norm business model where agencies keep a cut of their campaign fees, and produce the promotion results through paid placements. I've managed to build my network exclusively pitching to curators who are willing to be sent my music with no strings attached.
paragraphs.p4: Constraining the service to only include pitching curators for organic, earned placements in a music promotion landscape massively dominated by payola and fake endorsements means that we keep the entire campaign fee as profit less our administrative and technical costs. However, the value I provide to the curators I pitch is sending them music that they enjoy, suited to their taste.
paragraphs.p5: Another common strategy in the industry is casting a wide net, pitching to a broad range of curator-niches is also not feasible. Some of these curators receive hundreds of pitches per day, others a handful per month, but in both cases, sending music that's low quality or a poor genre fit one too many times will land all @braininavat.dance emails blocked or reported as spam.
paragraphs.p6: The model is only sustainable by maintaining a high quality roster of artists and record labels, and a high quality network of tastemakers open to considering unpaid placements.
paragraphs.p7: Because of this, a campaign is only taken on after understanding the music and the context around it, understanding the clients' goals for the release, and being confident I can create value for my client, as well as my network of curators.
paragraphs.p8: Every campaign crosses the same three high level systems: [kickoff](record:kickoff); [pitching](record:pitching); and [reporting](record:reporting). When you zoom in, this includes collecting assets and metadata from the client, researching and identifying bespoke targets, crafting and sending pitches, coordinating placements with curators and clients, collecting data documenting the campaign and its results, compiling reports, and communicating this to the client.
paragraphs.p9: This is a difficult operation to scale up without compromising the quality of the service on a purely operational level. But there are still many additional considerations.
paragraphs.p10: At first I thought it would be wise to focus my clientele within a narrow range of genres and offer services that cover only a narrow range of promotional media in order to multiply the potential placements I could earn for each pitch sent each week. However, I soon found that the campaigns were competing for a finite amount of openings that curator has for a given week. The alternative route is broadening the range of genres and media that I pitch, which adds many additional layers of operational complexity.

music-practice-automation.prompt: Close the record: automation, and what it freed up.

questions.q1: Automating much of the business in order to remove tedious labor, improve speed and quality of the service, and focus on high leverage creative and strategic judgements, client and curator relationships, iterating our existing processes, and building new ones.

systems-consulting.label: Brain in a Vat Systems & AI Consulting
systems-consulting.summary: Audit the operation, implement the high leverage opportunities, maintain and improve the systems.

paragraphs.p1: This can be anything from bespoke, purpose-built apps that replace expensive third-party software, to automated workflows that take the repetitive manual work off a team's plate, to AI systems built on properly structured data and context so they reliably produce good results.
paragraphs.p2: Each engagement starts by mapping how your team actually operates: what tools are in place, what's getting in the way, where work is still manual that shouldn't be. That becomes a prioritized, costed plan — what to build, in what order, and why — shaped with you. Then the build: standing up the systems and getting them live in your operations. And once they're running, the work keeps going: monitoring, tuning, and scaling what's there, plus new capability as the business grows.
paragraphs.p3: Two engagements are documented here as case studies: [a deal-stage and commission tracking tool for a real-estate team](record:real-estate), and [an artist/promoter tour advancing tool for an artist manager](record:touring).

kickoff.label: Music promo campaign kickoff
kickoff.summary: The keyboard shortcut that turns a client’s “let’s do it” into the correct Airtable records, Google Drive folders, Fillout form, a live invoice, a folder, and a drafted kickoff email in under a minute.

questions.q1: The moment: a signed confirmation means the client is ready to pay, and it is the worst time to disappear into administrative work.
questions.q2: One keyboard shortcut assembles the client and deal records, the invoice, the campaign folder, and a drafted kickoff email carrying a payment link and one asset-request form per campaign. Roughly thirty minutes across four apps became about one.
questions.q3: Restraint: the automation assembles and never commits. Every step is a prefilled dialog that can be cancelled, and the email stays a draft until sent.
questions.q4: The asset workflow: every asset lives on our side rather than as a link into the client's storage, assets we already hold are attached on the way out, nothing gets lost or stale, and the campaign starts while the client is still excited.

kickoff-sequence.purpose: Show the roughly thirty-minute, four-app administrative process collapsing into one guided sequence that still leaves commitment human.

questions.q1: The idea the system is built on: taste can be recorded, and recorded taste can drive targeting.
questions.q2: How it started: a spreadsheet of every curator's adds, passes, and feedback, and hundreds of pitch emails personalized by hand until mail merge made real segments possible.
questions.q3: What carries it now: one record per curator with their playlists rolling up underneath, at most one pitch per curator per week, a genre ontology shared by campaigns and playlists, and a weekly match that dedupes against every prior pitch into a draft list with its reasoning.
questions.q4: The one read kept human: whether a track reads commercial or underground, the call that sends two same-genre tracks to different playlists.
questions.q5: The backstops: reporting feeds missing genre tags back into the database, and every pitch links a playlist of all current campaigns so a curator can find the track I didn't send.

pitching-targeting-model.purpose: Make the curator records, playlist rollups, shared genre ontology, deduplication, and final human review gate inspectable as one system.

questions.q1: The cost: reporting once ate close to three days of every week, all of it collecting evidence of work already done.
questions.q2: The path: invented the process, refined it by hand for years, automated fragments with macros, then handed it to an assistant with no music background, which forced the judgment onto paper. Full automation is the same discipline with a faster executor.
questions.q3: Where the judgment lives now: a versioned rules document the model reads on every run (silence is not a pass, never invent, never downgrade an outcome), code that re-checks every conclusion, and the auto-pitchable decision kept outside the model in a small deterministic gate.
questions.q4: Today: the pipeline runs daily, dashboards refresh through the day, client emails arrive as drafts for a personal pass, and roughly sixteen hours of reporting per campaign became about an hour of my week.

reporting-pipeline.purpose: Trace the daily pipeline from source evidence through model judgment, deterministic verification, the auto-pitchable gate, dashboards, and drafted client reports.

real-estate.label: Real-estate deal tracker
real-estate.summary: A brokerage team's deal operation mapped end to end, with explicit stages and named owners, and a realtime dashboard created inside the Google tools they already use.

questions.q1: Before: a single deal crossed six tools between pitch and close, held together by the coordinator's attention, with agents tracking deals in notebooks and verbal updates so the record ran a step behind reality.
questions.q2: The operations map: the deal lifecycle as explicit stages, each with a named condition for advancing and a named owner for every hop between tools.
questions.q3: The constraints: the mandated brokerage platform has no API, and no new tools, so everything lives inside Google where the team already works.
questions.q4: The build: a realtime dashboard derived from the team's own spreadsheets. Once the states were on paper, the machine's share of the work was obvious.

touring.label: Tour advancing system
touring.summary: A tour-advancing system that turns one show record into role-specific forms, a day sheet, an artist calendar, and email drafts the manager reviews before sending.

paragraphs.p1: Advancing a show means assembling venue details, set times, riders, ground transport, hotels, and guest lists from people who each hold a different part of the answer. Promoters reply in email, artists text screenshots of flights, and the manager has to remember what is still missing. The day sheet is only as reliable as that memory.
paragraphs.p2: I started by making ownership explicit. A field registry names every piece of information, who supplies it, whether it is required, and where it should appear. The manager starts with a short intake: artist, date, artist email, and whether the routing includes hotel and transport. From there, the registry drives the manager view, promoter form, artist dashboard, day sheet, and missing-information logic. Each person sees the same show through the fields they own.
paragraphs.p3: That shared record renders the day-sheet PDF the team uses on show day, with venue, schedule, travel, and contact details pulled from the same source.
paragraphs.p4: When something is missing, the system drafts a reply in the existing promoter thread, in the manager's voice and addressed only to the promoter. It never sends.
paragraphs.p5: Confirmed arrival, departure, and set times become events in the artist's Google Calendar. Each event carries the venue, contact, and current day-sheet link. When a detail changes, the system updates these outputs instead of leaving them to drift apart.
paragraphs.p6: Running the system again does not create duplicate drafts, events, or PDFs. After a partial failure, it resumes from the last durable step. Past shows stay untouched, superseded files are removed, and the artist receives access to the PDF before its link appears in Calendar. The system works inside Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Sheets, where the manager already works.

yoohoo.label: Yoohoo
yoohoo.summary: Notifications that hold state: one durable record that agents, automations, and households can update, ask questions through, and resolve.

questions.q1: The problem: a push notification fires once and then rots. Yoohoo replaces it with one durable record per situation, where state updates in place, a question can go to several people and be answered exactly once, and the waiting workflow resumes with an authoritative result.
questions.q2: The model: the notification is a view and the server owns the record. The first valid answer wins, and a resolved question can never execute twice.
questions.q3: The line on AI: a model may draft content and quiet routine updates. It may never suppress a question, and it never decides authorization, recipients, or resolution. Every failure falls back to a deterministic path.
questions.q4: Status: specified. An approved product contract, awaiting implementation.

yoohoo-state.purpose: Show one durable server-owned record moving from open question through first valid answer to an exactly-once resolved state.

thread-from-argument-to-instrument.label: From argument to instrument
thread-from-argument-to-instrument.summary: A thread about the route from argument and operating work into software as a medium.

paragraphs.p1: The operating contexts and every software project compose this reading.

making-work-playable.title: Making work playable
making-work-playable.lede: The best work tools do more than remove steps. They become responsive enough to practice on and, eventually, to stop noticing.

questions.q1: The opening scene: a script that watches the dictation engine's log so the confirming keystroke lands the instant the transcript finishes pasting. An unreasonable amount of engineering for a quarter of a second, and the whole thesis: a tool you have to think about is a tool you are not thinking through.
questions.q2: What fluency does to a day: instant, trusted capture makes a stray idea stop being an interruption, cheap frequent actions make the right move and the easy move the same move, and work starts to reward repetition the way an instrument does.
questions.q3: Where each product holds the standard: Dubs as a thought captured mid-stride, Writ as a tool that passes by disappearing, Yoohoo as notifications that hold state without adding noise.

thread-playable-instruments.purpose: Reuse the strongest campaign, client-system, Dubs, Writ, and Yoohoo visuals as one sequence of tools becoming fluent enough to disappear.

questions.q1: INFAMOUS: inventing the services meant living their costs. Days went to compiling evidence of finished work and midnights to personalizing pitches by hand. The first instruments were small (text snippets, mail merge) but proved the shape of the work was something I could change.
questions.q2: The defining move was teaching: handing the reporting process to an assistant with no domain background forced me to define it better than I ever had for myself, and directing work from outside the weeds became the skill the rest runs on.
questions.q3: Independence compounded it: at Brain in a Vat there were no approvals to wait on and no inherited systems. The low-context executor became as often an AI agent as a person, and agent-driven automation matured into a real operating advantage built to my own judgment and taste.
questions.q4: The advantage became a second practice: consulting is doing for other teams what I did for my own operation, turning fuzzy workflows into explicit states and owners inside the tools people already use.
questions.q5: The products came from the same habit: Writ because my audio kept landing on the wrong device, Dubs because I was briefing agents from memory on walks. Neither started as a product; at some point I stopped treating the fixing as a distraction from the work.
questions.q6: The specs once written for a human assistant now go to agents, the same discipline with a faster executor. Software stopped being the tool that supported the work and became the medium the work happens in.

thread-from-argument-to-instrument.purpose: Recompose the strongest operating and product visuals as a chronological path from argument to software as the medium of the work.
